title: Thibault Formal (@thibault_formal) — thread (4 tweets)
summary:
[1/4] New sparse retrieval model: introducing SPLARE, which extends SPLADE by replacing the vocabulary head with pretrained SAEs!
paper: (ICLR'26)
also how we won the WSDM'26 Cup on multilingual retrieval: (model weights coming soon!)
────────
[2/4] TL;DR: SPLADE-like models are bottlenecked by their backbone's vocabulary — making training harder and multilingual/cross-lingual adaptation painful. Meanwhile, sparse models have fallen behind dense & multi-vector models on benchmarks like MTEB. Time to fix that!
────────
[3/4] This is preliminary work — lots left to explore: complementarity between standard and latent vocabularies, extension to multimodal settings, and more. Suggestions and feedback very welcome! cc @sclincha
────────
[4/4] Bonus: SAEs make training easier — query & doc vectors are already naturally sparse at initialization. They also give finer control over the vocabulary (number of tokens, modality, etc.). And features stay interpretable via mechanistic interpretability tools (see paper for details!)

title: Thibault Formal (@thibault_formal) — thread (12 tweets)
summary:
[1/12] Introducing SPARSEUP: the first model release from @Linkup_platform , and the missing sparse companion of DenseOn and LateOn.
Same backbone, same data, <150M, 56+ on BEIR-13. The model is open-source, use it!
Blog:
Model: (Apache 2.0)
────────
[2/12] A few months ago @LightOnIO released DenseOn & LateOn: open data, and a recipe that lets you compare architectures, all other things equal. SOTA models on BEIR, genuine generalization checked through decontamination. That recipe was meant to have a third seat at the table. cc @antoine_chaffin @raphaelsrty @AmelieTabatta @paulomouraj
────────
[3/12] Why? These models are less understood, and can be hard to train. A tokenizer vocab also makes multilinguality less natural, so they drifted out of the spotlight. Today's "SOTA sparse" still lags comparable dense and late-interaction models, which keep getting newer backbones and better data.
────────
[4/12] Learned sparse embeddings are a whole different class of models. Inverted-index retrieval, readable bags, precise lexical match (also they are just cool). Despite that, they are not as popular as dense retrieval. Few public models, even fewer open, which feels crazy next to the dense zoo.
────────
[5/12] We make a first contribution towards better sparse embedding models: we start from LightOn pre-trained checkpoint (LateOn-unsupervised), and derive a SPLADE-like model with a few simple but important modifications (details in the blog). We train on the same fine-tuning mixture, et voilà!
────────
[6/12] That’s a shame, esp. because late interaction puts sparse retrieval back on the map (SMVE, SSR, ColBERTSaR, etc.). There has never been a better moment to push the performance of LSR models!
────────
[7/12] On BEIR-13, SPARSEUP hits 56.4 nDCG@10: the first public vocab-based sparse encoder under 150M we know of to go above 56. SPARSEUP is contrastive only, no distillation.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSa41liXsAAZoj1.jpg
────────
[8/12] The more interesting comparison: all other things equal, late interaction still wins, especially OOD. SPARSEUP lands close to DenseOn but doesn’t close the gap - decontaminated looks closer, but that average is noisy. Not the late interaction > sparse > dense story we were expecting.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSa5GLCWIAAwrR-.jpg
────────
[9/12] Anyway, the model is cool, and purposely sparse (it’s possible to gain a few points by inflating L0 but we didn’t go this route). When combined with Seismic, it can reach sub-ms on MS MARCO (single-threaded), at >97% recall vs exact search. cc @fmnardini @rventurini_ @cosimorulli1 @SilvioMartinico
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSa5evlW4AAbaek.png
────────
[10/12] This is the first release from Linkup Research - more to come!
Thx @antoine_chaffin for the finding the name (and the many discussions), @tomaarsen for answering questions about Sentence Transformers (yes, it is ST-compatible). Enjoy!
────────
[11/12] As usual, you can inspect the bags. Pretty cool, and underrated imo.
We also added a cheap attribution method: max-pooling maps each output dim back to the input word that produced it. Loose importance, but you can see how the model operates.
“These examples look dumb, I don’t want to use the model!” They do. That’s the point. You can see the corner cases. Dense fails too - you just assume it’s smart.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSa6A_mWYAAwp1M.png
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSa6A_sXQAAPtIs.jpg
────────
[12/12] @antoine_chaffin @tomaarsen and special thx to @cosimorulli1 who performed the crazy seismic evaluations!
